items.stem: Which of the following best describes "selection"?
options: Google's original ranking algorithm (Page and Brin, 1998) that rates a web page's importance by the number and quality of links pointing to it
Decisions made by algorithms with little or no human involvement, such as automatic loan approvals
A search that checks each item in a list in turn until the target is found or the list ends
A control structure in which a decision (e.g. IF…THEN…ELSE) determines which instructions are carried out
items.answer: A control structure in which a decision (e.g. IF…THEN…ELSE) determines which instructions are carried out
items.markingKey: D. "selection" is a control structure in which a decision (e.g. IF…THEN…ELSE) determines which instructions are carried out.

items.stem: Briefly explain why algorithms must be unambiguous.
items.answer: Computers follow instructions exactly and cannot interpret vague steps, so each step must have one clear meaning; ambiguity leads to errors or different results each time.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Computers follow instructions exactly and cannot interpret vague steps, so each step must have one clear meaning; ambiguity leads to errors or different results each time. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: A student claims: "Algorithms are only found in computers." Identify the error in this claim and correct it.
items.answer: An algorithm is any precise set of steps – recipes, long division and route directions are algorithms; computers execute algorithms at speed and scale.
items.markingKey: An algorithm is any precise set of steps – recipes, long division and route directions are algorithms; computers execute algorithms at speed and scale. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem:
An array LIKES holds likes on each post: [30, 17, 29, 17] (indexes start at 0).

TOTAL = 0
loop I from 0 to 3
    TOTAL = TOTAL + LIKES[I]
end loop
output TOTAL

Trace the algorithm and state the output.
With reference to the UK A-level grading algorithm (2020), explain how it illustrates how algorithm design determines outcomes.
items.answer: With exams cancelled, Ofqual used an algorithm based on schools' past results and teacher rankings; about 39% of teacher-assessed grades were lowered, and after protests the government reverted to teacher grades. Using historical school performance as an input meant individual students at historically lower-performing schools were downgraded, showing that design choices embed values.

items.answer: Designers choose goals, inputs, weightings and definitions of success, so algorithms reflect human judgements and values rather than being neutral or objective.

items.answer: Inputs: membership status, number of books on loan, overdue fines; selection: IF member AND loans < limit AND fines = 0 THEN allow ELSE refuse; output decision. Unfairness: e.g. a fixed fine rule excludes low-income members; no human override. Reward correct structure and evaluation.

items.stem: "Everyone in a digital society needs to understand how algorithms work." How far do you agree? Refer to at least one Digital Society concept in your answer.
items.answer: A basic algorithmic literacy is important for citizens, but accountability must not be shifted to individuals who cannot see inside proprietary systems.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: algorithms shape news, jobs and finance; understanding helps people challenge unfair decisions. Arguments against: many algorithms are proprietary and secret; responsibility should lie with designers and regulators, not individuals; basic literacy matters more than technical detail. items.stem: Briefly explain why decomposition is useful when designing an algorithm for a real-world system.
items.answer: Breaking a large problem (e.g. a food-delivery app) into smaller parts (matching, routing, pricing, payments) makes each part easier to design, test and improve, and lets teams work in parallel.

items.stem: Explain why algorithms are central to digital society.
items.answer: Algorithms automate decisions that affect people – what news they see, who gets a loan, which driver gets a job – at huge scale, so their design shapes opportunities and power in society.

items.stem: Explain the difference between iteration and selection.
items.answer: Selection chooses which path to follow based on a condition (IF…THEN); iteration repeats a block of instructions (loops) while or until a condition holds.

items.stem: Evaluate the claim: "Algorithms make fairer decisions than humans."
items.answer: Algorithms can be more consistent, but fairness depends on design, data and oversight; they are not inherently fairer than humans.

items.stem: With the help of a specific example, explain why binary search is faster than linear search on large sorted lists.
items.answer: Each comparison halves the remaining items, so the number of steps grows with log₂ n (about 20 for a million items) instead of n (up to a million for linear search). (A specific, correct example that illustrates this is required for full marks.)

items.answer: Automation can support welfare administration, but final decisions with serious consequences need human review, transparency and easy appeal.

items.stem: Which of the following is an example of a false negative?
options: A spam filter lets a genuine email through
A spam filter lets a phishing email into the inbox
A spam filter blocks a genuine email from a friend
A spam filter blocks a spam email
items.answer: A spam filter lets a phishing email into the inbox
items.markingKey: B. A real positive was missed.

items.stem: Explain the difference between a false negative and a false positive.
items.answer: A false positive wrongly flags something as positive (an innocent person flagged as a fraud risk); a false negative wrongly misses a real positive (a fraud that goes undetected).
items.markingKey: A false positive wrongly flags something as positive (an innocent person flagged as a fraud risk); a false negative wrongly misses a real positive (a fraud that goes undetected). items.stem: Outline one way in which spam filters in email services shows accuracy and error trade-offs.
items.answer: Gmail and other services use machine-learning filters to classify billions of emails as spam or not each day. Tuning the filter to catch more spam (fewer false negatives) increases the chance that genuine emails are hidden (false positives), so designers must choose which error matters more.
items.markingKey: Context (Gmail and other services use machine-learning filters to classify billions of emails as spam or not each day.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. items.stem: Outline one way in which Robodebt (Australia, 2016–2019) shows risks of automated decision-making.
items.answer: Services Australia's automated system compared averaged tax-office income with welfare records and issued debt notices; many debts were wrong, and a Royal Commission (2023) called the scheme "crude and cruel". Removing human checks and reversing the burden of proof meant a flawed calculation was applied to hundreds of thousands of people, causing financial and psychological harm.
items.markingKey: Context (Services Australia's automated system compared averaged tax-office income with welfare records and issued debt notices; many debts were wrong, and a Royal Commission (2023) called the scheme "crude and cruel".) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. items.stem: Which of the following best describes "collaborative filtering"?
options: An output that wrongly flags something as present or positive, such as an innocent person flagged as a fraud risk
An algorithm that orders results (search results, posts, products) according to calculated relevance or other criteria
A finite, ordered set of unambiguous instructions for solving a problem or completing a task
A recommendation method that suggests items liked by users with similar behaviour ("people who watched this also watched…")
items.answer: A recommendation method that suggests items liked by users with similar behaviour ("people who watched this also watched…")
items.markingKey: D. "collaborative filtering" is a recommendation method that suggests items liked by users with similar behaviour ("people who watched this also watched…").

items.stem: State what is meant by the term "efficiency".
items.answer: How much time (number of steps) and memory an algorithm needs as the size of its input grows
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the core idea: how much time (number of steps) and memory an algorithm needs as the size of its input grows. Award full marks only if the defining feature is clear; a vague example alone scores 0.

items.stem: Distinguish between selection and iteration.
items.answer: Selection chooses which path to follow based on a condition (IF…THEN); iteration repeats a block of instructions (loops) while or until a condition holds.
items.markingKey: Selection chooses which path to follow based on a condition (IF…THEN); iteration repeats a block of instructions (loops) while or until a condition holds. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Explain the difference between linear search and binary search.
items.answer: Linear search checks items one by one and works on unsorted lists but is slow for large lists; binary search repeatedly halves a sorted list and is much faster but requires the data to be sorted first.
items.markingKey: Linear search checks items one by one and works on unsorted lists but is slow for large lists; binary search repeatedly halves a sorted list and is much faster but requires the data to be sorted first. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Explain why accuracy alone is not enough to evaluate an automated decision system.
items.answer: An accurate system can still produce many harmful errors if cases are imbalanced, and errors may fall unevenly on certain groups; the type of error (false positive vs negative) and who bears it matter as much as the overall rate.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: An accurate system can still produce many harmful errors if cases are imbalanced, and errors may fall unevenly on certain groups; the type of error (false positive vs negative) and who bears it matter as much as the overall rate. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Explain why the design of a ranking algorithm is a source of power.
items.answer: Most users click the first few results, so whoever designs the ranking decides which businesses, news and views get attention, shaping markets and public opinion.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Most users click the first few results, so whoever designs the ranking decides which businesses, news and views get attention, shaping markets and public opinion. items.stem: Kwame writes: "Automating a decision always makes it more efficient and therefore better." Explain why this is inaccurate.
items.answer: Automation can be faster, but if the algorithm is inaccurate or biased it spreads errors at scale (Robodebt raised hundreds of thousands of unlawful debts); efficiency is not the same as quality or fairness.
items.markingKey: Automation can be faster, but if the algorithm is inaccurate or biased it spreads errors at scale (Robodebt raised hundreds of thousands of unlawful debts); efficiency is not the same as quality or fairness. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem:
Read the source below.

"The algorithm did not see me. It saw my school's history."
— Student from a state school in northern England, interviewed by a newspaper after A-level results, August 2020

With reference to the source, explain how the inputs of an algorithm can lead to unfair outputs.
items.answer: The algorithm used the school's past results as an input, so an individual's grade depended on others' historical performance rather than their own work; inappropriate inputs produced unfair individual outcomes.
items.markingKey: The algorithm used the school's past results as an input, so an individual's grade depended on others' historical performance rather than their own work; inappropriate inputs produced unfair individual outcomes. items.stem:
Read the source below.

"More than 70% of the time people spend watching YouTube is driven by our recommendation algorithms."
— Neal Mohan, YouTube Chief Product Officer, interview with CNET, 2018

Explain what the source suggests about the power of recommendation algorithms.
items.answer: Most viewing is chosen by the algorithm rather than direct search, so the platform's design largely decides what users watch and which creators succeed.
items.markingKey: Most viewing is chosen by the algorithm rather than direct search, so the platform's design largely decides what users watch and which creators succeed. Award marks for points drawn explicitly from the source; own knowledge alone is not credited in this part.

items.stem:
Read the source below.

"The scheme was a crude and cruel mechanism, neither fair nor legal, and it made many people feel like criminals."
— Royal Commission into the Robodebt Scheme, Final Report, Australia, 2023

With reference to the source, explain two impacts of the automated decision system.
items.answer: It produced unfair and unlawful debts (legal and financial impact), and it caused psychological harm by making people feel like criminals (social/emotional impact).

An array TIMES holds delivery times in minutes: [22, 34, 18, 33, 10] (indexes start at 0).

BEST = TIMES[0]
loop I from 1 to 4
    if TIMES[I] > BEST then
        BEST = TIMES[I]
    end if
end loop
output BEST

Trace the algorithm and state the output.
items.markingKey: BEST takes values 22 → 34 → 34 → 34 → 34 [M1]; output 34 [A1].

items.stem:
A music-streaming app ranks items with the score = 0.6 × match to listening history + 0.3 × number of plays + 0.1 × newness (each rated 0–10).
Item X: match to listening history 10, number of plays 7, newness 3
Item Y: match to listening history 4, number of plays 5, newness 4
Item Z: match to listening history 3, number of plays 2, newness 2
Calculate the score for each item and state which is recommended first.
Using spam filters in email services as an example, explain accuracy and error trade-offs.
items.answer: Gmail and other services use machine-learning filters to classify billions of emails as spam or not each day. Tuning the filter to catch more spam (fewer false negatives) increases the chance that genuine emails are hidden (false positives), so designers must choose which error matters more.
items.markingKey: Context (Gmail and other services use machine-learning filters to classify billions of emails as spam or not each day.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: tuning the filter to catch more spam (fewer false negatives) increases the chance that genuine emails are hidden (false positives), so designers must choose which error matters more. – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to accuracy and error trade-offs.

items.stem: With reference to the Uber matching algorithm, explain how it illustrates inputs, processes and outputs.
items.answer: Uber's system takes inputs such as rider location, driver locations, traffic and demand, and outputs a driver assignment, an estimated arrival time and a price (including surge pricing). The algorithm transforms location and demand data into decisions that affect drivers' income and riders' costs, showing how algorithmic outputs shape people's lives.

items.stem: Analyse one strength and one limitation of this view: "Recommendation algorithms benefit users more than they benefit platforms."
items.answer: Users gain convenience, but algorithms are optimised for platform goals; benefits to users are real but secondary unless users get control (e.g. DSA non-profiling feed option).
items.markingKey: Arguments for: help users find relevant content among millions of items; save time and support discovery of niche creators. Arguments against: designed to maximise engagement and advertising revenue; can narrow exposure and promote extreme content; users have little control or transparency. Supported judgement: Users gain convenience, but algorithms are optimised for platform goals; benefits to users are real but secondary unless users get control (e.g. DSA non-profiling feed option).

items.stem: With reference to two real-world examples, discuss the claim that the most important quality of an algorithm is its efficiency.
items.answer: Efficiency is necessary for scale, but in decisions about people, accuracy, fairness and accountability are more important.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: efficiency enables services at the scale of billions; reduces energy and cost. Arguments against: accuracy and fairness matter more when decisions affect people; efficient but biased systems spread harm quickly. Supported judgement: Efficiency is necessary for scale, but in decisions about people, accuracy, fairness and accountability are more important. Markbands [8]: 7–8 – well-developed evaluation of impacts/implications, specific real-world example(s), balanced and with a supported conclusion; 5–6 – evaluation with relevant example(s) but uneven balance; 3–4 – some relevant points, mainly descriptive, conclusion asserted; 1–2 – limited, general response.

items.stem: With reference to two real-world examples, discuss the claim that algorithms make fairer decisions than humans.
items.answer: Algorithms can be more consistent, but fairness depends on design, data and oversight; they are not inherently fairer than humans.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: consistent rules applied to everyone; not affected by mood, fatigue or personal prejudice. Arguments against: learn and reproduce historical bias (Ofqual 2020, COMPAS); opaque and hard to challenge; consistency can spread one error to thousands of people.
